newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algeria votes law to impose Arabic, curb French.
newsitem.headline: Algeria votes law to impose Arabic, curb French.

text.p: Algeria's government-appointed quasi-parliament, the Transitional National Council, passed on Tuesday a new law banning officials from making public statements in any language other than Arabic.

But the Council's members, shown on Algerian state-run television massively voting the law by a show of hands, dropped a requirement in the initial law obliging foreign firms to seal deals with Algeria in the Arabic language.

The change, underpinning the Algerian authorities' efforts to attract foreign investors to the violence-torn oil and gas producing North African country, allows partners to have contracts signed in two languages, with both regarded as official.
Under the law, officials who write or sign memos or correspondences in foreign languages, can be fined up to 5,000 dinars ($91) or up to 10,000 dinars ($182) if they reoffend.

The measure, which will result in curbing French, used by most officials in senior economic and government positions, has worried the Algerian elite, including editors and journalists in Algeria's leading French-language newspapers.
But the law gave a reprieve for French-speaking Algerians by stating "the process of generalising the use of the Arabic language should be perfected by July 5, 1998."
Teaching in schools and universities in Arabic must be in place by July 5, 2000, the text of the law says.
Algeria's leaders, in a constant drive to boost the Arab-Moslem people identity, have been keen on promoting the Arabic language since independence from France in 1962 after 132-year occupation.
Secular opposition leaders, backed by French-speaking intellectuals, allege that speedy Arabisation helped Moslem militancy taking roots in the country.
About 60,000 people have been killed in Algeria's violence since early 1992 when the authorities cancelled a general election which radical Islamists were poised to win.
